transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?
I guess… it’s something at work. When I see balloons at the school, even from down the hallway, I sort of freeze up. My chest gets tight right away, and it takes me a moment to think straight again.
Does this reaction to balloons happen to you in other places outside of work?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid close attention outside of school… I guess I mostly notice it there.
Does the reaction to balloons happen when you see them in pictures or videos, outside of the school setting?
I haven’t really noticed it much with pictures or videos. It’s more when I actually see them at school… like even across the hallway, I just tense up and kind of freeze for a second.
Has anything significant or traumatic happened to you at school that involves balloons?
Yes… I mean, I don’t know if I’d call it traumatic, but about seven months ago a balloon burst really close to my face during a kids’ art celebration. Since then it’s been… harder.
Do you often feel anxious or nervous in situations that don't involve balloons?
Not really… I mean, I get stressed like anyone, but I haven’t noticed that same nervous feeling unless it’s about balloons.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or events because you think there might be balloons there?

Yeah… a little. I’ve been asking my aides to handle birthday circles sometimes. And if there are festival tables with balloons, I’ll kind of move away. If I can’t, I just keep my distance and try not to look at them until it’s over.
Are there any activities or daily routines that you've stopped doing or changed because of your reaction to balloons?

Yeah… mostly at work. I’ve had to let my aides take over some normal classroom celebrations, like birthdays. And there was a festival art table I was supposed to help with, but I didn’t… my supervisor noticed that.
Have you ever had a moment where you felt an intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, with symptoms like a racing heart or shortness of breath?

Yeah… it happens pretty fast. If I see balloons at school, even down the hall, my chest kind of tightens and I freeze for a second. It takes me a bit before I can think about what I’m supposed to be doing.
Do you think you would have the same reaction to balloons if you saw them at your home?

I’m not totally sure. I think it’s worse at school… like the second I spot them, even across the hallway, I tense up and kind of freeze for a moment. At home, I guess I’d probably still feel it, but I’m not around them there much.
Do you think your reaction to balloons would be less intense if you saw them in a different setting outside of school?

Maybe a little, but… I don’t think it would go away. I know it’s probably just decoration, but if I see one stretched tight or bobbing around, especially near kids, I get scared it’s going to pop right in my face. It feels bigger than it should.

Do you think you would have the same intense fear reaction to balloons if you were to see them in a different setting, like a store or a park, that has no connection to your work or the past incident?

I think it might still happen, yeah. Maybe I’d try to tell myself it’s different, but if I spot balloons, I tend to tense up right away… my chest tightens and I kind of freeze before I can think clearly.
Do you think your reaction to balloons would be the same if you saw them at a friend's house?

I think… probably not exactly the same, maybe, but I’d still react. Like if I saw balloons there, I’d tense up right away. At school it’s more immediate for me — even seeing them down the hall, my chest tightens and I kind of freeze before I can think.
Do you think you would have the same intense fear reaction to balloons if you were in a situation where you knew for sure that the balloons could not pop or make a loud noise?

If I really knew it couldn’t pop or make a sound… maybe it wouldn’t be as bad. But I think seeing it stretched tight or moving near the kids would still make me scared for a second, like it’s going to burst right in front of me, even if I know that doesn’t make sense.
Do you think your reaction to balloons would be just as intense if you saw them in a situation that is similar to the one where the balloon burst, but not at school?

Yeah… I think if it felt similar, it could still hit me pretty fast. At school, even seeing balloons across the hallway makes my chest tighten and I kind of freeze for a moment before I can think. So somewhere similar… probably, yes.
Do you think your reaction to balloons would be significantly less intense or even absent if you knew you would never see them at school again?

Maybe less, yes… if I knew they wouldn’t be at school, that would help. But the part that really gets me is when I spot them there — even across the hallway — my chest tightens and I sort of freeze before I can think what I’m supposed to do.
Would your fear of balloons completely go away if you never had to go back to that school again?

No… I don’t think it would completely go away. Maybe school makes it worse, but even somewhere else, if I saw a balloon stretched tight or bobbing near kids, I’d still get that feeling like it could burst right in my face. It feels bigger than it should.
Would your reaction to balloons be the same if you were to see them in a different school?
I think… probably, yes. If it was still at a school and I saw balloons, even down the hallway, I’d get that same tight feeling in my chest and sort of freeze for a second before I could think.
Would your reaction to balloons be less intense if you were teaching at a different school?

Maybe a little, if it was a different place… but I think if I saw balloons there, I’d still react right away. It’s like the second I notice them, my chest tightens and I freeze for a moment before I can think.
Would your reaction to balloons be the same if you were to see them in a different classroom within the same school?
Yes… I think it would be about the same. Even if it’s just a different classroom, if I spot balloons, my chest tightens right away and I kind of freeze before I can think clearly.
